definition.text: Parametric, or index-based, insurance pays a pre-set amount when a measured trigger, such as a wind speed or rainfall level, is reached.

facts.text: Ordinary indemnity insurance pays the assessed loss after an event; parametric insurance only checks that the trigger was passed, using weather services, sensors or satellites.
Its main benefit is fast payout, giving cash for recovery soon after a disaster, and lower transaction costs.
Its main drawback is basis risk: payouts follow parameters, so they may not cover the full damage.
Mexico's Quintana Roo insures a coral reef with a wind-triggered policy paying up to $3.8 million a year; Hurricane Delta in 2020 triggered an $850,000 payout.
Pooled schemes such as the Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility, set up in 2007, let countries buy cover more cheaply than alone.

title: Social finance

definition.text: Social finance is financial services that use private capital to tackle social and environmental needs while giving investors a return.

facts.text: Unlike philanthropy, it sustains itself by being profitable for investors rather than relying on donors.
It has no agreed definition but includes impact investing, socially responsible investing and lending to social enterprises.
It grew quickly after the 2008 financial crisis as investors sought ethical alternatives.
Critics argue it pulls capital from productive uses, while backers say it adds direct investment where charity is declining.
It struggles with low returns, high start-up and regulatory costs, neglect by mainstream banks and poor access to retail investors.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether social finance adds value beyond corporate social responsibility or simply diverts capital.

title: Social impact bond

definition.text: A social impact bond is an outcomes-based contract in which private investors fund a public programme and the government repays them only if agreed goals are met.

facts.text: Unlike ordinary bonds, they have no fixed return; payment depends on social outcomes.
The first, launched in the UK in 2010, funded prisoner rehabilitation at Peterborough Prison.
By 2022 there were 276 projects with $745m raised, used in 23 countries as of May 2023.
Backers say taxpayers pay only for success; critics say they displace other funding and are an expensive way to run programmes.

contested_note: Advocates say social impact bonds reward success, while critics say they displace funding and cost more.

definition.text: A sustainability bond is a bond whose money must fund a mix of green and social projects.

facts.text: Green, social and sustainability bonds differ in which project categories the money may go to; sustainability bonds must combine both.
The ICMA principles are the most widely accepted framework for issuing all three kinds.
Critics warn of greenwashing because no single definition says what makes a bond sustainable.
